title: Growing kale microgreens
subtitle: Sturdy brassica cotyledons with a nutty flavour, ready in 8 to 12 days
excerpt: Kale microgreens grow more slowly than radish or broccoli but produce robust, dark green cotyledons with a nutty, mild brassica flavour. Sow on a 25 cm tray, blackout for three days, then give good light for 5 to 9 more days before cutting.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: The seed leaf that emerges first when a seed germinates. In microgreen growing, the cotyledon stage is the harvest window: fully-expanded seed leaves with no true leaves yet showing.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Kale microgreens are a year-round indoor crop sown on a 25 cm tray. The cycle is 8 to 12 days: sow, cover and blackout for three days, then bring to a bright position for the remaining 5 to 9 days until the
are fully expanded. Kale cotyledons are darker green and more substantial than broccoli, with a nutty, mild brassica flavour that works in salads and grain bowls.

Kale grows slightly more slowly than radish or broccoli at the microgreen stage, which means the blackout window is longer and the tray needs good light for most of its second week. This is a reliable crop in summer; in winter, a grow light makes a material difference to yield and uniformity.

Light source: a bright south-facing windowsill in summer is sufficient. In winter, a supplementary LED grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray, running 14 to 16 hours a day, produces the best results. Kale microgreens in low winter light grow pale and thin; they still germinate but the texture and colour at harvest are noticeably inferior.
Ambient temperature: 18 to 22°C. Kale tolerates slightly lower temperatures than basil or coriander but grows noticeably slower below 15°C. A warm kitchen counter is a good position year-round.

Day 0: sow. Fill a 25 cm tray with pre-dampened seed compost or coir to within 1 cm of the rim. Level and firm lightly. Scatter kale seed at 15 to 20 g per tray. The seed is small; distribute it evenly with a shaker motion from 20 to 30 cm above the surface. Press gently into contact with the medium.

Days 1 to 3: blackout. Stack a second tray on top and weight it flat. Remove when shoots are 2 to 3 cm tall. With kale, this blackout phase typically runs a full three days because the seeds germinate slightly more slowly than radish.

Days 4 to 12: light and watering. Move to a bright position. Cotyledons green up within 24 hours. Water from below only: set the growing tray inside a second tray with 1 to 2 cm of water and allow the medium to absorb it. Check every day; kale medium can dry out faster than broccoli in a warm room.

Days 8 to 12: cut. Cotyledons should be fully expanded, standing upright, and 5 to 8 cm tall. Cut with scissors 1 cm above the medium. Do not wait for the first true leaves, which develop unevenly and signal the end of the best flavour window.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting the tray
attrs.intro: Common problems in kale microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Stems rot at the base, tray smells musty
items.cause: Damping off from overwatered or stagnant medium.
items.fix: Bottom-water only and do not allow standing water to remain in the outer tray overnight. Add a small fan nearby to improve airflow. Discard and restart.

items.symptom: Slow germination, tray sparse after day 5
items.cause: Old seed stock, cold room temperature, or medium too dry during germination.
items.fix: Check the ambient temperature is above 15°C. Keep the medium consistently damp during the blackout phase. Test seed viability before a full batch.

items.symptom: Pale, thin stems after moving to light
items.cause: Insufficient light during the growing phase.
items.fix: Move to a brighter window or add a grow light. Kale needs more light than radish to produce a good green colour and upright stems.

items.cause: Surface moisture from top-watering or poor airflow.
items.fix: Bottom-water only. Run a small fan at low speed near the tray. The mould is on the substrate, not the stems; the cotyledons remain safe to cut.

content.text: Use untreated kale seed. Garden centre kale seed often carries a fungicide coating; check before buying. Microgreen suppliers sell untreated kale in larger packs.
risk is low for kale. Bottom-water only and keep air moving around the tray.
